name: 5-HTP (oxitriptan)

lead: 5-HTP is the step between tryptophan and serotonin and is sold as a supplement for sleep and mood. Looksmaxxing users take it for deeper, longer sleep, which they connect to clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face.

The body makes it from tryptophan; it crosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted to serotonin, an effect raised by decarboxylase inhibitors such as carbidopa. Human trials are registered for depression, mood, body composition, fatigue, satiety and sleep, but the sources reviewed do not report outcomes and none targets appearance.

paras: People take it as capsules, usually in the evening as part of a sleep routine, and sometimes in bedtime stacks with magnesium. Effects on sleep are judged over days to weeks.
Serotonin syndrome is a documented concern when combined with serotonin-raising drugs such as SSRIs. No FDA-approved medicine contains 5-HTP as of 2025, and it is sold as a supplement.

angle.text: 5-HTP is taken as a serotonin precursor for mood and sleep, on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. Trials cover mood and sleep, among other conditions; none address appearance.

lead: 5-Hydroxytryptophan (5-HTP), known medically as oxitriptan, is a naturally occurring amino acid and the intermediate step between tryptophan and serotonin. The body makes it from tryptophan through tryptophan hydroxylase, the rate-limiting step in serotonin synthesis, and unlike serotonin itself it crosses the blood-brain barrier [1][2]. Food contains only insignificant amounts [1]; commercial supplements are generally sold as capsules and tablets.

In looksmaxxing and fitness circles 5-HTP is treated as a sleep and recovery supplement. The reasoning is a chain: serotonin is a precursor to melatonin, better and more consistent sleep supports recovery, and recovery supports training, skin and overall appearance. Lifters on the T Nation forum mention it alongside melatonin, magnesium and ashwagandha as something to try for insomnia or for winding down after hard training [3][4].

Research on 5-HTP focuses on mood, sleep, appetite and neurological conditions. A 2006 review examined the double-blind trials in depression [5], a 2004 toxicology review examined its safety record [6], and registered trials have looked at sleep quality in older adults, body composition, satiety and fatigue [7][8][9][10]. Wikipedia notes that, as of 2025, no FDA-approved medicines contain 5-HTP [1].

paras: The sleep use rests on biochemistry: 5-HTP is converted to serotonin, which is further transformed to melatonin, and the synthesis of 5-HTP from tryptophan is the limiting step for both [2]. A 12-week randomized trial in older adults in Singapore tested daily 5-HTP supplementation against no supplementation and measured sleep with questionnaires and actigraphy, alongside serotonin, melatonin and gut microbiota markers [11]. A 2023 review of complementary approaches to sleep problems in children and adolescents lists 5-HTP among adjunctive interventions that clinicians have used [12].

Medically, oxitriptan has been used for depression and some other indications, particularly in Europe [1][5]. Earlier clinical work also used it, with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor, in myoclonus [13]. Registered trials examine it for satiety in obesity, fatigue in inflammatory bowel disease remission, and ADHD-related traits [9][10][14].

Tryptophan hydroxylase converts tryptophan to 5-HTP, and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, with vitamin B6 as a cofactor, converts 5-HTP to serotonin in nervous tissue and the liver [1]. Because serotonin cannot cross the blood-brain barrier but 5-HTP can, oral 5-HTP bypasses the rate-limiting enzymatic step [1][5].

How much 5-HTP reaches the central nervous system depends on how much is converted to serotonin in the body's periphery, and that conversion can be blocked by peripheral decarboxylase inhibitors such as carbidopa [5]. The effect is also potentiated by benserazide, and an investigational oxitriptan/carbidopa combination exists [1].

In rodents, very high 5-HTP exposure produces a serotonin syndrome and a head-twitch response used as a laboratory proxy for psychedelic-like effects. Wikipedia reports that this has not been observed in humans, and the rodent doses are orders of magnitude above human supplement amounts [1]. Older pharmacology studies used 5-HTP to probe serotonin receptor behaviours in mice and rats [15].

Serotonin syndrome, which can include hallucinations, has been reported with overdoses of serotonin-elevating drugs, and combination with other serotonergic medicines is the context where it is discussed [1][5]. Reviews of 5-HTP safety examine eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (EMS), which led to the withdrawal of L-tryptophan supplements in 1989 after being traced to a contaminated batch from one manufacturer [6]. A 2004 toxicology review concluded that, in two decades of worldwide use, no definitive cases of toxicity had emerged beyond one unresolved case, and that analyses of 5-HTP sources had found no contaminants like those in the tryptophan episode [6]. Users on forums describe next-day tiredness, flatness or reduced drive to train with nightly use [4][16].

5-HTP appeared in clinical research in the 1970s, including a 1971 trial in Down syndrome, a Japanese therapy report from 1972, a 1976 trial combining it with carbidopa in myoclonus, and a 1978 study in autistic children [17][18][13][19].

The supplement boom followed a safety crisis in a related product. In November 1989 the first cases of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (EMS) in people taking L-tryptophan supplements were reported to the US CDC; more than 1,500 cases and at least 37 deaths were eventually linked to the outbreak, which investigators tied to L-tryptophan from a single large Japanese manufacturer whose recent batches contained trace impurities [20]. The FDA recalled tryptophan supplements in 1989 and restricted most public sales in 1990, loosening the restrictions in 2001 and the import limits in 2005 [20]. After the ban, 5-HTP, a normal metabolite of tryptophan, became a popular replacement supplement for people seeking serotonin support [6][20].

A 2004 toxicology review by Das and colleagues looked back at roughly twenty years of worldwide 5-HTP use and reported that no definitive cases of toxicity had emerged apart from one unresolved Canadian case, and that analyses of several 5-HTP sources had not found the contaminants associated with the tryptophan episode [6].

A 2006 review by Turner, Loftis and Blackwell covered preclinical and clinical evidence for 5-HTP in depression, emphasising double-blind, placebo-controlled trials and examining EMS and serotonin syndrome as the main safety issues. It also discussed how peripheral decarboxylase inhibitors such as carbidopa change how much 5-HTP reaches the brain [5].

The most direct recent study of the sleep use is a single-blinded, 12-week randomized trial published in 2024 in 30 older adults in Singapore (mean age about 66), who took 100 mg of 5-HTP daily or no supplement. Sleep was assessed every four weeks with the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and actigraphy, and blood serotonin, urinary melatonin, gut microbiota and stool short-chain fatty acids were measured at weeks 0 and 12 [11]. The authors report that 5-HTP raised serum serotonin and had a favourable effect on certain sleep-quality components, with the clearest improvement in the subgroup of poor sleepers, and that gut microbiota composition also improved in that group. They note that the small sample limits generalisation [11].

ClinicalTrials.gov lists further studies on sleep quality and gut microbiome [7], body composition [8], exercise and cortisol [21], mood and emotional processing in healthy volunteers [22], satiety in obesity [9], fatigue in inflammatory bowel disease remission [10], major depression combined with creatine [23], ADHD traits [14], pediatric asthma [24] and spinal cord injury [25]. No registered study found tests it for appearance outcomes.

On T Nation, 5-HTP is a recurring suggestion in threads about insomnia, including for people with sleep disruption after starting testosterone therapy and after intense workouts [3][4][26]. Experiences vary: one member writes that it works well for sleep but leaves them too relaxed the next day, another stopped a nightly routine because of daytime tiredness, and another reports it did not help [4][16][27]. Wikipedia lists medical brand names used in Europe, and in the US it is sold as a dietary supplement [1].

lore.intro: Forum members discuss 5-HTP mainly as a sleep aid and mood supplement, usually in lists with melatonin, magnesium and ashwagandha [3][4][26].
